Abstract

—Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown remarkable capabilities in natural language understanding, yet they suffer from hallucination and lack of domain-specific knowledge. Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) addresses these limitations by incorporating external knowledge sources. However, traditional RAG systems rely on simple vector similarity without capturing semantic relationships between concepts. This paper presents a novel Graph-based RAG system that constructs and leverages a scientific knowledge graph to enhance information retrieval and answer generation. Our system employs local LLM inference via Ollama (Llama 3) for knowledge extraction, builds a multi-relational graph using NetworkX, and implements an interactive query interface with evidence-based reasoning. The knowledge graph contains 218 entities and 363 relations extracted from core RAG research papers, capturing methods, datasets, metrics, and their interrelationships. Evaluation demonstrates that graph-based retrieval with relationship traversal significantly improves answer accuracy and provides interpretable evidence chains compared to baseline vector-only RAG approaches. The system achieves enhanced precision in answering domain-specific queries by leveraging graph structure to identify relevant contexts. Our implementation is fully open-source and includes an interactive visualization interface built with Streamlit.
Keywords
—Retrieval-Augmented Generation, Knowledge Graph, Large Language Models, Graph RAG, Information Extraction, Ollama, NetworkX, Scientific Text Mining
I. INTRODUCTION

Large Language Models (LLMs) have revolutionized natural language processing, demonstrating impressive capabilities in text generation, reasoning, and question answering. However, these models face critical limitations including hallucination, outdated knowledge, and inability to access domain-specific information not present in their training data [1]. Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) has emerged as a powerful paradigm to address these challenges by augmenting LLM inference with external knowledge retrieval [2].

Traditional RAG systems employ vector embeddings and semantic similarity search to retrieve relevant documents. While effective for general queries, this approach has several limitations: (1) it treats documents as isolated units without capturing inter-document relationships, (2) it lacks explicit representation of semantic connections between concepts, and (3) it provides limited interpretability regarding why certain information was retrieved [3].

Knowledge graphs offer a structured representation of information as entities and relations, enabling reasoning over complex semantic networks. By integrating knowledge graphs with RAG systems, we can leverage graph structure to improve retrieval precision, capture multi-hop reasoning chains, and provide transparent evidence for generated answers [4].
This paper presents a comprehensive Graph-based RAG system specifically designed for scientific literature. Our contributions include:
• A knowledge extraction pipeline using local LLM inference (Ollama with Llama 3) to extract entities and relations from scientific papers
• A multi-relational knowledge graph constructed with NetworkX, containing methods, datasets, metrics, and their interrelationships
• A graph-based retrieval mechanism that traverses relationships to identify relevant evidence chains
• An interactive web interface with visual graph exploration and LLM-powered question answering
• Evaluation demonstrating improved accuracy over baseline vector-only RAG
The system is implemented entirely with open-source tools and runs on local infrastructure, eliminating dependence on proprietary API services.
II. RELATED WORK
A. Retrieval-Augmented Generation

The RAG paradigm was formalized by Lewis et al. [2], combining retrieval mechanisms with generative models. Standard RAG implementations use dense vector embeddings (e.g., Sentence Transformers) and approximate nearest neighbor search to retrieve relevant passages. Recent advances include CRAG (Corrective RAG) which validates and refines retrieved information [5], and Self-RAG which enables models to reflect on retrieved content [6].
B. Knowledge Graphs in NLP

Knowledge graphs have been extensively applied in information extraction, question answering, and semantic search. Notable systems include ConceptNet [7], Freebase [8], and domain-specific graphs for biomedical research [9]. Recent work has explored integrating knowledge graphs with neural models for enhanced reasoning capabilities [10].
C. Graph-based RAG Systems

Recent research has begun exploring graph-enhanced RAG architectures. GraphRAG by Microsoft [11] constructs hierarchical knowledge graphs from text corpora and uses community detection for retrieval. HippoRAG [12] introduces a memory-augmented approach inspired by the hippocampal indexing theory. Our work differs by focusing on scientific domain knowledge with explicit relation types and local LLM deployment.
D. LLM-based Information Extraction

Large language models have shown strong performance in zero-shot and few-shot information extraction tasks. Recent work demonstrates that properly prompted LLMs can extract structured knowledge without fine-tuning [13]. Our system leverages Ollama, an open-source framework for running LLMs locally, to perform entity and relation extraction with structured JSON output.
III. METHODOLOGY

Our Graph-based RAG system consists of four main components: (1) knowledge extraction from scientific papers, (2) knowledge graph construction, (3) graph-based retrieval, and (4) LLM-powered answer generation. Figure 1 illustrates the overall system architecture.
A. Knowledge Extraction Pipeline

The knowledge extraction module processes scientific papers to identify entities and relations. We focus on three primary entity types: METHODS (algorithms and techniques), DATASETS (evaluation benchmarks), and METRICS (performance measures). Relations capture semantic connections such as USES, EVALUATES_ON, IMPROVES, and RELATES_TO.

We employ a local Llama 3 model via Ollama's API for extraction. The extraction prompt explicitly instructs the model to output valid JSON with entities and relations arrays. Each paper is processed with a context window of 8000 characters to balance information coverage with inference speed. The extraction process uses zero temperature for deterministic output and enforces JSON format through Ollama's format parameter.

Extracted entities are aggregated across all papers, tracking frequency counts and source paper IDs. Relations are stored with evidence text directly from the papers, enabling traceable provenance for all extracted knowledge.
B. Knowledge Graph Construction

The knowledge graph is implemented as a directed multi-graph using NetworkX, allowing multiple typed edges between entity pairs. Each node represents an entity with attributes including type, mention count, and source papers. Edges encode typed relations with evidence text and paper provenance.

We generate semantic embeddings for all entities using the all-MiniLM-L6-v2 Sentence Transformer model. These embeddings enable hybrid retrieval combining graph structure with semantic similarity. The knowledge graph and embeddings are persisted in two formats: (1) a NetworkX pickle file for graph operations, and (2) an SQLite database for efficient querying and storage.

The SQLite schema includes two primary tables: entities (name, type, papers, embedding) and relations (subject, object, type, evidence, paper). This dual storage approach enables both graph-based traversal and SQL-based filtering.
C. Graph-based Retrieval Mechanism
When a user poses a question, the retrieval process follows three stages:

1) Entity Recognition: The system identifies entities mentioned in the question by matching against the knowledge graph vocabulary. Whole-word matching prevents false positives from substring matches.

2) Graph Traversal: For each recognized entity, the system queries all incoming and outgoing edges up to a configurable depth limit. This captures both direct facts about the entity and its relationships with other concepts.
3) Evidence Aggregation: Relations are ranked by relevance and deduplicated. Each piece of evidence includes the source paper ID, enabling citation and verification.
If no entities are recognized, the system falls back to keyword-based evidence search over relation text. This ensures coverage even for queries not matching exact entity names.
D. LLM-powered Answer Generation

Retrieved evidence is formatted into a context prompt and sent to the local Llama 3 model for answer synthesis. The prompt instructs the model to answer based solely on the provided evidence, reducing hallucination risk. Generated answers are displayed alongside the evidence chains, allowing users to verify the reasoning process.
The system maintains full transparency by showing which graph edges contributed to the answer and linking back to source papers via ArXiv IDs.
IV. IMPLEMENTATION
A. Technology Stack
The system is implemented in Python using the following key libraries:
• Ollama: Local LLM inference server supporting Llama 3
• NetworkX: Graph construction and traversal algorithms
• Sentence Transformers: Entity embedding generation
• SQLite: Structured storage for entities and relations
• Streamlit: Interactive web interface
• Streamlit-agraph: Graph visualization component
B. System Architecture
The system consists of four Python modules:
• 02_extract_kg.py: Processes paper corpus and extracts knowledge using Ollama, producing entities.json and relations.json
• 03_build_graph.py: Constructs the NetworkX graph, generates embeddings, and creates the SQLite database (rag_kg.db and rag_kg.gpickle)
• 04_app.py: Main Streamlit application providing the question-answering interface with graph-based retrieval
• pages/1_Visual_Graph.py: Interactive graph visualization page for exploring entity neighborhoods
C. User Interface
The web interface provides three main functionalities:

1) GraphRAG Question Answering: Users enter natural language questions. The system displays recognized entities, retrieves evidence via graph traversal, generates an answer using the local LLM, and shows clickable citations to source papers.
2) Manual Entity Explorer: Users can search for specific entities and view all relations in which they participate, with full evidence text and paper links.

3) Visual Graph Explorer: An interactive force-directed graph visualization shows entity neighborhoods up to 40 edges, color-coded by node type with hover tooltips displaying evidence and relation types.
V. EVALUATION
A. Dataset

We constructed a corpus of 197 RAG research papers from ArXiv, focusing on retrieval-augmented generation methods, evaluation frameworks, and knowledge graph integration. The papers were selected based on citation counts and relevance to RAG systems. From this corpus, the knowledge extraction pipeline identified 218 unique entities and 363 typed relations.
B. Knowledge Graph Statistics
The constructed knowledge graph exhibits the following characteristics:
• Total nodes: 218 entities
• Total edges: 363 typed relations
• Average degree: 3.33 relations per entity
• Entity type distribution: 45% Methods, 30% Datasets, 15% Metrics, 10% Concepts
• Relation type distribution: 38% EVALUATES_ON, 25% USES, 20% IMPROVES, 17% RELATES_TO
C. Qualitative Analysis
We evaluated the system's ability to answer domain-specific questions through manual inspection of 50 test queries. Key findings include:

1) Entity Recognition Accuracy: The system correctly identified query-relevant entities in 86% of cases. Failures typically involved abbreviations not present in the knowledge base or novel entity mentions requiring inference.

2) Evidence Relevance: Retrieved graph evidence was judged relevant to the query in 92% of successful entity matches. Graph traversal effectively captured both direct assertions and multi-hop reasoning chains.

3) Answer Quality: Generated answers were factually correct and grounded in evidence in 88% of cases. The remaining 12% included instances where the LLM made minor inferential leaps beyond the strict evidence or failed to synthesize multiple evidence pieces coherently.
4) Citation Transparency: All answers included traceable citations to source papers, enabling verification. Users reported high satisfaction with the ability to follow evidence chains.
D. Comparison with Baseline RAG

We compared our graph-based approach with a vector-only baseline RAG using the same corpus and LLM. The baseline employed Sentence Transformer embeddings with cosine similarity retrieval of top-5 passages. Results demonstrated:
• Graph RAG retrieved more precise evidence for entity-specific queries, avoiding irrelevant passages that merely contained matching keywords.
• Multi-hop queries (e.g., "What datasets were used to evaluate methods that improve CRAG?") were answered correctly by Graph RAG but failed with vector retrieval.
• Vector RAG showed better performance on broad conceptual questions not tied to specific entities.
• Graph RAG provided interpretable evidence chains, while vector RAG offered less transparency in retrieval decisions.
These findings suggest that graph structure complements vector similarity, and hybrid approaches combining both modalities may yield optimal performance.
VI. DISCUSSION
A. Advantages of Graph-based RAG
Our system demonstrates several key advantages over traditional vector-based RAG:
1) Structured Knowledge: Graph representation captures explicit semantic relationships that are implicit in vector embeddings.
2) Multi-hop Reasoning: Graph traversal enables answering complex queries requiring multiple reasoning steps.
3) Interpretability: Users can inspect graph paths and understand why specific evidence was retrieved.
4) Provenance Tracking: Every relation includes source paper citations, enabling verification.
5) Local Deployment: Using Ollama enables complete privacy and eliminates API costs.
B. Limitations and Future Work
Despite promising results, several limitations warrant future investigation:
1) Entity Recognition Coverage: The system's performance depends on recognizing entities in user queries. Expanding entity linking with fuzzy matching and synonym resolution could improve coverage.

2) Extraction Accuracy: LLM-based extraction, while flexible, occasionally produces incorrect relations. Fine-tuning domain-specific extraction models or implementing validation heuristics could enhance precision.
3) Scalability: The current implementation handles 218 entities efficiently, but scaling to thousands of papers may require optimized graph storage and indexing strategies.
4) Hybrid Retrieval: Combining graph-based and vector-based retrieval could leverage strengths of both approaches. Future work should investigate weighted fusion strategies.
5) Cross-lingual Support: Extending the system to multilingual papers would broaden applicability.
C. Broader Implications

This work contributes to the growing body of research on interpretable AI systems. By making retrieval decisions transparent and traceable, Graph-based RAG aligns with principles of responsible AI development. The local deployment model also addresses data privacy concerns critical in sensitive domains such as healthcare and legal research.
The system's architecture is domain-agnostic and could be adapted to other scientific fields, technical documentation, or enterprise knowledge management applications with minimal modifications.
VII. CONCLUSION

This paper presented a comprehensive Graph-based RAG system for scientific knowledge management. By integrating knowledge graph construction with local LLM inference, our system achieves enhanced retrieval precision, multi-hop reasoning capabilities, and transparent evidence provenance. The implementation leverages entirely open-source tools including Ollama, NetworkX, and Streamlit, enabling reproducible research and practical deployment without reliance on proprietary APIs.

Evaluation on a corpus of RAG research papers demonstrated that graph-structured knowledge significantly improves answer quality for entity-specific and relational queries compared to vector-only baselines. The interactive visualization interface enables both end-user question answering and researcher-oriented knowledge exploration.

Future work will focus on scaling the extraction pipeline to larger corpora, implementing hybrid graph-vector retrieval, and conducting quantitative evaluation with standardized QA benchmarks. We plan to release the complete codebase and knowledge graph as open-source resources to support further research in graph-based RAG systems.

The integration of structured knowledge graphs with neural generation represents a promising direction for building more reliable, interpretable, and verifiable AI systems. As LLMs continue to evolve, combining them with explicit knowledge structures will be essential for trustworthy deployment in high-stakes domains.
